About us
Every company has a mission. What's ours? To empower every person and every organization to achieve more. We believe technology can and should be a force for good and that meaningful innovation contributes to a brighter world in the future and today. Our culture doesn’t just encourage curiosity; it embraces it. Each day we make progress together by showing up as our authentic selves. We show up with a learn-it-all mentality. We show up cheering on others, knowing their success doesn't diminish our own. We show up every day open to learning our own biases, changing our behavior, and inviting in differences. Because impact matters. 

Microsoft operates in 190 countries and is made up of approximately 228,000 passionate employees worldwide.

Last night we opened a door unlike any other. At the heart of Microsoft’s campus, step into the new home of the
UW's Global Innovation Exchange
(GIX) and you cross from
Microsoft
into the
University of Washington
. No one has ever put a great research university and a leading technology company under the same roof quite like this. As far as I know, no one has even tried.

The timing matters. Artificial intelligence is advancing fast. The question is whether the people building it understand the world it’s changing. This calls for a new style of education and leadership. We need leaders who understand the technology deeply and see things through other people’s eyes. Leaders who learn by collaborating on real projects with people from different countries and disciplines.

That’s what GIX is built for. Students will learn from faculty across the UW, take classes taught by Microsoft employees, and be mentored by people from across our industry here in the Pacific Northwest. And it works both ways. Our first cohort of 30 senior technical leaders from Microsoft will spend their evenings here in a mini-MBA program, and our goal is three or four cohorts every year.

This partnership will do great things for our two institutions, for our state, and as a role model beyond Washington. What we have today is strong. But what’s to come will be even greater.

So many people made this possible. Thank you to UW President
Robert J. Jones
, who saw that this could matter even more in the future than it does today, and to academic leaders across the university. To the incredible Microsoft team for backing and building this from the very beginning. To Redmond Mayor Angela Birney and our state legislators. To Christine Gregoire, who helped find a path forward when we needed one, and to
Sean Carr
, who has nurtured GIX into what it is today.

The New Bottleneck
The bottleneck is no longer intelligence.

Over the last six months, intelligence has accelerated dramatically. But smarter models are not enough for everyone to benefit from novel intelligence. New form factors are required.

GPT-3 needed Chat. 
Opus 4.5 needed Code and Cowork.

Today, with Astra and Fable, we’re in a familiar position. Intelligence is advancing faster than it can reach people in useful forms. The model overhang is back.

The new bottleneck is
diffusion
. Increased intelligence needs to translate to human progress.

Microsoft’s mission is to empower every person and every organization to achieve more. If we fail to create new ways to utilize increased intelligence, this mission is at risk.
The New Copilot
Our next step is the new Copilot. Home, Code, and Autopilot.
Home
is your new starting point, unifying Chat and Cowork into a single experience. Ask a quick question or delegate a whole project. No need to decide where to start.

Home also features Today, our new proactive view that spans Outlook, Teams, meetings, and tasks. Today doesn’t just flag things you missed; it moves work forward. The draft is already written, and the schedule change is already proposed.

We’re also bringing Office into Copilot. For the first time, you don’t have to choose between AI editing and human collaboration. We’ve brought the full power of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint into Copilot, so you can create, edit, and collaborate with colleagues and Copilot at the same time.

Next,
Code
is coming to Copilot. Models can write code but environments, hosting, and sharing get in the way. With Code, just describe an app, tracker or workflow in plain English. Code runs sandboxed on your machine or safely in your tenant in the cloud. Now, hosting and sharing an app is as easy as a Word document.

Finally,
Autopilot
. Your digital teammate. Give it a name, an appearance, a role, and a goal. Your Autopilot has it’s own identity, memory, computer, and workspace. Autopilot is enterprise grade, with real permissions, audit, and governance, all from Agent365. It can monitor work, coordinate with your team, and keep projects running over weeks -- just tag it in a document, forward it an email, or message it on Teams!

Home. Code. Autopilot.

Intelligence is here. Put it to work.

We've long argued for a balanced approach to AI regulation. One that keeps humans in control. Since 2023,
Microsoft
has advocated for "safety brakes" or an “off switch" that keeps advanced AI systems under human control. And it should ensure that AI systems that control critical infrastructure and autonomous systems be run in secure cloud infrastructure with layered safeguards that provide additional intervention points as needed. Put simply, powerful AI systems should always remain under human control, including interruption, correction, and shutdown.

This approach is tried and tested. In the 1850s, Elisha Otis’ demonstration of a safety brake at the World’s Fair helped earn the public’s trust – and made modern cities possible. We should adopt this principle for AI. If we do, AI can become a powerful tool for human progress. If we don't, a lack of public trust, not regulation, will become the limiting factor that slows AI adoption.

I've seen many periods of significant change over the course of my career. This moment feels different, not only because of how quickly AI is advancing, but because of the choices it asks leaders to make about how work changes and how people grow with it.
 
No organization has all the answers. What we can bring is a growth mindset: the willingness to experiment, learn from what doesn’t work, and keep adapting as the technology and our understanding of it evolves.
 
That’s why we committed to being Customer Zero. If we want to help customers realize the full value of AI, we need firsthand experience with the hard, deeply human work of transformation.
 
Today, we’re sharing more of that experience in
Microsoft
’s Frontier Playbook, drawing on hundreds of AI transformation efforts across the company. It includes what worked, where we failed, and how those lessons are changing the way we lead, build skills, and redesign work.
 
We’re still learning. But by sharing what we’ve learned so far, I hope we can help more organizations approach this moment with both ambition and humility, while creating a future in which technology helps people and organizations do more than they could before.

I share five lessons from our journey in my latest blog:

As AI advances, so must the work to ensure its developed and used responsibly. The latest Responsible AI Transparency Report looks at how we're strengthening the policies, practices, and governance needed to help ensure AI remains worthy of people's trust.
Natasha Crampton
1mo
Today, we published our 2026 Responsible AI Transparency Report. 
  
One of the clearest lessons from our work is that responsible AI governance is not a destination. It’s an ongoing discipline that must evolve alongside the technology itself. 
  
This year’s report shares how we’ve re-engineered our Responsible AI Standard to address emerging AI capabilities, strengthened our risk-based approach to governance, and continued to translate what we’re learning into the tools, practices, and processes that help operationalize responsible AI across Microsoft. 
  
While technology continues to evolve, our AI principles remain a constant foundation. They guide how we approach new challenges, evaluate risks, and build accountability into our work.
  
Transparency is an important part of that process. By sharing our progress, challenges, and lessons learned, our goal is to contribute to stronger AI governance across the broader ecosystem.
  
No organization can do this alone. Advancing responsible AI will require continued collaboration, shared learning, and collective action across industry, government, academia, and civil society.
  
I encourage you to learn more about the report here:
https://lnkd.in/ekStFTyg
